summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on unit economics. We reviewed current tokens/sec/$, caching wins from prefix caching, and tradeoffs when increasing batch sizes. Agreed to run two more batch configs and to get a representative prompt set from customer. Action items assigned; next run target is to simulate Dedicated-like reserved capacity for latency comparison.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, well keep this tight — 45 minutes. quick roll call?
[00:07] Tommy Nguyen: Tommy here, cto, lena and priya on my side as well.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: Lena ON, hi.
[00:15] Priya Rao: Priya, SRE lead.
[00:18] Arjun Patel: Arjun from Redwood, SE. Diego on audio but muted.
[00:23] Maya Chen: Great. Agenda: quick recap of last runs, tokens/sec per dollar, caching observed, then tuning plan. Arjun, you want to open with the numbers?
[00:32] Arjun Patel: Sure. So baseline run using redwood-hosted medium model variant gave about 1,200 tokens per second across the pool, that's observed on our perf harness. When we convert to tokens per dollar under current pilot credits and the VM mix, that's roughly 45k tokens per dollar for the default quantized build. caveat: this includes a lot of short prompts which inflate throughput.
[00:55] Tommy Nguyen: Wait 45k? that seems high compared to our internal numbers, we saw 28k on similar load. Are you including KV cache hits?
[01:03] Arjun Patel: Good call — the 45k includes prefix caching from the K-V cache we enabled. When cache hits excluded we're ~27k, so that aligns closer to your 28k. our previous slide deck (shared: drive.google.com/bench/kestrel-bench) shows the breakdown.
[01:20] Lena Ortiz: The K-V cache seems very sensitive to prompt similarity. Our workload has a lot of template overlap, so we expect high cache hit rates in production, but there are bursts of unique queries.
[01:30] Maya Chen: Right — so we highlighted two numbers: tokens/sec with caching and tokens/sec without caching, and unit econ should use both for conservative planning.
[01:38] Arjun Patel: On caching savings: in the last 24-hour sample from your pilot traces we saw ~62% effective token savings from prefix reuse. That translated into about 1.6x cost reduction in that window. note, transcription might flip percent signs but that's the gist.
[01:55] Priya Rao: 62% sounds promising. did you test eviction behaviour? we have rolling 7-day data retention and some heavy tail prompts.
[02:03] Arjun Patel: We tested with synthetic tail and saw hit rate drop to ~35% for tail-heavy windows; eviction TTL in our sim was 6 hours. we can tune TTL for Dedicated.
[02:15] Tommy Nguyen: On batching: weve been cautious because our SLA is 200ms p95. Increasing batch size usually increases throughput but hurts p95.
[02:25] Diego Morales: (muted) yep — tradeoff graph is in the doc, batch=1 p95 is about 160ms, batch=8 p95 jumps to ~420ms on same instance class. throughput improved ~2.4x though.
[02:38] Lena Ortiz: so what do you recommend? we need a mix of low-latency for interactive flows and high-throughput for async scoring.
[02:46] Arjun Patel: We recommend hybrid routing: low-latency requests routed to smaller batch/low-queue instances, async scoring batched aggressively. Redwood routing policy can do this — we demoed it earlier.
[02:58] Priya Rao: Any quick wins on cost with minimal latency impact?
[03:02] Arjun Patel: Prefix caching is the biggest immediate win for you given template overlap. Also small model variants for non-critical scoring can reduce cost 20-30% with modest accuracy drop. quantization profile shift (8-bit) also reduces memory and improves throughput — tradeoffs documented.
[03:20] Maya Chen: I pushed an annotated sheet showing the per-route token economics with two columns: conservative (no cache) and optimistic (observed cache). Thats what well send after this call.
[03:30] Tommy Nguyen: On Dedicated vs Hosted: you mentioned simulating Dedicated — how close does hosted simulate reserved capacity?
[03:37] Arjun Patel: We can run a Dedicated-like config in our hosted environment by reserving a pool for your pilot and constraining autoscaling, that gives similar queue dynamics. For strict SLA and network isolation you'd move to Redwood Dedicated or Private.
[03:50] Lena Ortiz: Network is a concern for us — we need KMS + SSO and private egress. Priya can detail the firewall constraints later.
[03:58] Priya Rao: We need to ensure egress to redwood endpoints over TLS through our proxy, and KMS via customer-managed HSM is preferred.
[04:06] Arjun Patel: Noted. we support KMS integrations and can do SAML SSO. Diego, we should capture the network team contact.
[04:12] Diego Morales: Will do.
[04:14] Maya Chen: Quick check on numbers: arjun, can you summarize the delta between batch configs youre proposing?
[04:20] Arjun Patel: Sure. baseline batch=1: p95 160ms, tokens/sec 1,200. batch=8: p95 420ms, tokens/sec 2,900. batch=16: p95 610ms, tokens/sec 3,900. effective tokens/$ improves linearly-ish, but user-facing latency at p95 doubles/triples. Theres also memory/kv cache interplay — larger batches increase KV cache pressure.
[04:45] Tommy Nguyen: For interactive chat wed probably cap batch at 4; for nightly scoring maybe 16.
[04:52] Arjun Patel: That pattern makes sense. Also note quantized model variants have slightly lower p95 at the same batch but sometimes lower quality. we'll surface sample outputs in the spreadsheet.
[05:03] Lena Ortiz: Any anomalies in error rates during the runs?
[05:06] Arjun Patel: Error rates stayed under 0.2% except a throttle spike during a synthetic concurrency ramp — caused by a misconfigured burst limit in the harness. not production-y, but were re-running to be sure.
[05:18] Maya Chen: Next steps recap: Arjun to run batch=8 and 16 on your real prompt set and send logs. Lena to share 48 hour prompt trace. Maya to send annotated cost model. Priya to share KMS/SAML contact.
[05:30] Tommy Nguyen: timeline ok — well prioritize the prompt trace. one question: are there guardrails for fallback to cheaper model when quality drop detected?
[05:40] Arjun Patel: Yes, Redwood routing supports model-fallback policies and A/B rollouts; we can tie it to a quality metric and auto-fallback if hallucination score crosses a threshold. we recommend a small canary first.
[05:52] Priya Rao: About security docs — can you share SOC2 and encryption in transit / at rest details?
[05:58] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 attestation, our data handling whitepaper, and the KMS integration guide in the follow-up.
[06:06] Diego Morales: Ill also include a short runbook for the simulated dedicated run we plan.
[06:10] Lena Ortiz: Cool, that helps.
[06:12] Tommy Nguyen: If we can get the batch runs before Friday we can start internal perf gating.
[06:18] Maya Chen: Got it. Any other Qs?
[06:20] (brief pause)
[06:25] Priya Rao: Curious about cost predictability — is there tooling for forecasting tokens/dollars per route week-over-week?
[06:31] Arjun Patel: Redwood Console has per-route token burn reporting and a monthly forecast based on recent windows; we can also export a CSV for your billing forecasts.
[06:40] Lena Ortiz: ok great, thanks.
[06:43] Maya Chen: Alright, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and scheduling for the dedicated-like run. Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[06:50] Tommy Nguyen: Thanks all.
[06:52] (meeting ends)
